questions.question: What is methylmercury and how do I get exposed to it from food?
questions.answer: Methylmercury (MeHg) is the organometallic form of mercury that biomagnifies up aquatic food chains and dominates dietary mercury exposure in people who eat fish. For non-occupational populations, exposure is dominated by fish consumption, with large long-lived predatory fish such as shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish, and bigeye tuna carrying the highest loads because they accumulate the metal over their lifespan. Marine mammals like whales and seals, eaten in some subsistence and indigenous diets, are among the highest-MeHg foods documented [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle & Barchowsky 2021]].

questions.question: Why is methylmercury considered especially risky during pregnancy?
questions.answer: Methylmercury crosses both the placenta and the blood-brain barrier, and fetal exposure during gestation produces developmental neurotoxicity at levels well below those causing overt symptoms in adults, making the fetus, breastfed infant, and young child the principal at-risk populations. The FDA/EPA fish-consumption advisory specifically targets pregnant women and women of childbearing age because in-utero exposure is the most consequential exposure window [[sources/fda-epa-fish-consumption-advice|FDA 2017]]. The dose-response anchoring most advisories comes from the long-running Faroe Islands and Seychelles birth-cohort studies.

questions.question: Which fish are highest and lowest in methylmercury?
questions.answer: MeHg concentration follows trophic level: large, long-lived predatory fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel, Gulf of Mexico tilefish, bigeye tuna) carry the highest loads because they bioaccumulate the metal over their lifespan. Smaller short-lived fin-fish such as sardines, anchovies, herring, salmon, trout, and tilapia carry substantially less, and shellfish carry less than similarly sized fin-fish due to lower trophic position and shorter lifespan. Because of this, choosing lower-trophic species is the dominant lever for reducing dietary MeHg exposure [[sources/li2024-global-fisheries-mehg|Li et al. 2024]].

questions.question: What regulatory limits and intake guidelines apply to methylmercury?
questions.answer: Binding maximum levels include the EU Reg. 2023/915 species-specific mercury limits for fishery products (applied as total mercury on the assumption that most mercury in fish is methylmercury) and Codex methylmercury maximum levels for fish, while the FDA sets a nonbinding action level of 1.0 ppm methylmercury in fish [[regulations/eu-2023-915|EU Reg. 2023/915]]. For tolerable intake, EFSA set a Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake of 1.3 µg/kg bw/week [[sources/efsa-mercury-methylmercury-2012|EFSA 2012]] and JECFA set 1.6 µg/kg bw/week [[sources/jecfa-61st-methylmercury|JECFA 2004]], while EPA's IRIS reference dose of 0.1 µg/kg bw/day (about 0.7 µg/kg bw/week) is the most conservative [[sources/epa-iris-methylmercury|EPA IRIS 2001]].

questions.question: Can I be exposed to methylmercury from foods other than fish, like rice?
questions.answer: Yes. Rice is the second-most-important dietary methylmercury source after fish, particularly in Asian populations with low fish but high paddy-rice consumption. Rice grown in contaminated soils (for example artisanal-gold-mining-impacted or chlor-alkali-contaminated watersheds) can carry MeHg in the 5 to 50 µg/kg range, with extreme cases exceeding 100 µg/kg [[sources/brombach2017-methylmercury-european-commercial-rice|Brombach et al. 2016]]. One rural-China cohort found that rice-derived maternal MeHg exposure was associated with child neurodevelopmental endpoints independent of the fish pathway [[sources/rothenberg2021-maternal-methylmercury-rice-child-neurodevelopment-china|Rothenberg et al. 2021]].

questions.question: How is methylmercury exposure measured or tested for?
questions.answer: Hair mercury is the main long-term biomarker: it reflects systemic exposure over the 2 to 3 months before sampling and runs about 250 times the simultaneous whole-blood level because methylmercury binds preferentially to cysteine residues in keratin. Whole-blood mercury reflects recent (days-to-weeks) exposure and is used clinically and in pregnancy monitoring, while urine mercury mainly reflects inorganic mercury, not MeHg [[sources/martinez-morata-2023-metal-biomarkers-state-of-science|Martinez-Morata et al. 2023]]. In food, speciation methods such as GC-ICP-MS or LC-ICP-MS directly quantify MeHg, while total-mercury methods like CV-AFS or TDA-AAS are used where the MeHg-to-total-Hg ratio is well characterized.
